newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland should curb widening trade gap - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Poland should curb widening trade gap - analyst.

text.p: Poland is firmly on a growth track but it will have to prevent the widening trade gap from depleting foreign reserves and hampering future foreign debt repayments, a government analyst said on Wednesday.

Tadeusz Chroscicki, the chief analyst at the Centre for Strategic Studies, said consumer demand would continue to fuel this year's economic growth, which should reach at least 5.5 percent, compared with an estimated six percent in 1996.

He told a news conference that the government's goal of slashing inflation to 13 percent in December from last year's 18.5 percent was within reach mainly thanks to an expected slower growth of food prices.
"Food prices growth should not exceed 10 percent in 1997...which should slow down inflation," he said.

But Chroscicki said that even though economic recovery expected in Poland's main trading partners should boost exports, trade gap was still likely to increase to at least $12 billion from last year's $8.2 billion and $1.8 billion in 1995.

"If the budget assumptions that imports will increase 21 percent and exports 15 percent this year prove true... the trade gap will rise to $12 billion," he said, adding however he thought these foreign trade targets were too ambitious.

He said that the mounting trade gap was likely to start eroding Poland's foreign currency reserves, which ought to be kept at a high level considering the country's foreign debt servicing and repayment obligations.
"In 1996 the reserves growth slowed, this year we should see no growth....Unless we do something about exports and imports they will start falling," he said.

He said high currency reserves were needed especially in 2004-2007 when Poland is due to pay its creditors between $4 billion and $5 billion annually in line with the 1993 debt reduction agreement with commercial banks.
"(With low reserves) it will not be easy to meet these payments," he said.

But he said exports, which rose less than seven percent in 1996, might begin to grow more robustly in mid-term as the current high level of investment, supported mainly by imports, improves competitiveness of the economy.
Chroscicki also said that Poland's economy was not overheating as some analysts suggest and that consumer demand and credit expansion, which ballooned last year, were under control.
The consumption of households was likely to grow about 4.5 percent in 1997, compared with an 8.1-percent increase last year, he said.
He said he saw room for two interest rate cuts by the central bank in 1997 if inflation would be falling as planned.

He said the unemployment rate, at 13.5 percent in January, was estimated to have risen to 13.6 percent in February and was forecast to fall to 12.4 percent at the end of 1997. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
